concepts.title: What a Real Quantum Computer Is
concepts.simple_explanation: A physical device whose qubits are real quantum systems, controlled by hardware (microwave pulses, lasers, magnetic fields, optics) and read out by measurement electronics. Its result for each run is a string of classical bits.
concepts.why_it_matters: Only hardware can run quantum circuits "natively" and, once large and reliable enough, offer speedups that classical simulation cannot match.
concepts.how_it_works: A circuit is translated ("compiled") into the device's native gates and qubit connections, executed by physically acting on the qubits, and then measured. Each execution gives one outcome string; repeating many times (shots) builds up a histogram. Several physical platforms exist (for example superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic systems, spin systems in semiconductors); they differ in speed, connectivity and error behaviour, and the landscape changes quickly.
concepts.visual_explanation: A pipeline: circuit → compile to native gates → control electronics/lasers → qubits → measurement → bit-string. A label shows "one random outcome per shot; noise present".
concepts.technical_explanation: Hardware qubits suffer decoherence and gate/readout errors; the executed operation is only an approximation of the ideal unitary circuit.
concepts.example: Running the Bell-state circuit on hardware 1000 times yields counts mostly at 00 and 11, plus a small number of 01 and 10 outcomes caused by errors.
concepts.common_mistake: Imagining a quantum computer returns exact probabilities or amplitudes. It returns only sampled bit-strings.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Applies Topic 1.2 (measurement gives one outcome) and Topic 1.3 (NISQ devices are noisy).
concepts.try_it: Compare an "ideal" and a "hardware-style noisy" result for the same circuit (Activity A03).
concepts.key_takeaway: A quantum computer is a physical machine that produces noisy, sampled classical outputs from real qubits.

concepts.title: What a Quantum Simulator Is (and the Terminology Trap)
concepts.simple_explanation:
A quantum circuit simulator is classical software that computes the effect of quantum circuits mathematically. The word "simulator" is overloaded, so three different things must be kept apart:
• Quantum circuit simulator — classical software mimicking a quantum circuit (the subject of this topic).
• Quantum simulation (of physical systems) — the *task* of modelling molecules or materials (Topic 1.3, C04), which can be attempted on a quantum computer.
• Analog quantum simulator — a purpose-built physical quantum system (such as cold atoms in a lattice) engineered to mimic another quantum system. It is real quantum hardware, not a program.
concepts.why_it_matters: Misreading these terms leads to confusion such as "a quantum simulator is a quantum computer" or "quantum simulation can be done on my laptop simulator at any size".
concepts.how_it_works: A circuit simulator represents the quantum state as numbers in memory and applies each gate as a matrix operation. Different simulator designs exist (C03, C07).
concepts.visual_explanation: A Venn-style diagram with three labelled circles — "circuit simulator (software)", "quantum simulation (the task)", "analog quantum simulator (special hardware)" — with short examples in each.
concepts.technical_explanation: Circuit simulators are deterministic classical programs; any randomness in their output comes from a pseudo-random number generator used for sampling shots.
concepts.mathematical_representation: |ψ_after⟩ = U_m ⋯ U_2 U_1 |ψ_0⟩   (the simulator multiplies the state by each gate's matrix in turn)
concepts.example: "Run my circuit on the simulator" means run it on a classical program; "simulate a molecule" means the physics task; "analog simulator" refers to a lab experiment.
concepts.common_mistake: Treating the three meanings as one.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Refers back to Topic 1.3 C04 (simulating quantum systems).
concepts.try_it: Sort example sentences into the three meanings (Activity A01, part 3).
concepts.key_takeaway: In this course, "quantum simulator" means classical software that computes what a quantum circuit does; it is not quantum hardware.

concepts.title: State-Vector Simulation and Why It Doesn't Scale
concepts.simple_explanation: A state-vector simulator stores all 2ⁿ amplitudes of the n-qubit state and updates them for each gate.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the standard, most transparent simulator: it is exact (up to rounding), gives full access to amplitudes, and mirrors the maths taught in this course. Its limit is memory and time.
concepts.how_it_works:
Start with |00…0⟩ (amplitude 1 for the all-zero string, 0 elsewhere). For each gate, multiply the affected parts of the vector by the gate's matrix. A single-qubit gate updates pairs of amplitudes; a two-qubit gate updates groups of four. Each gate touches essentially all 2ⁿ amplitudes, so work per gate also grows like 2ⁿ. At the end, probabilities are |amplitude|²; shots are drawn from those probabilities.
Memory: with one 128-bit complex number (two 64-bit floats) per amplitude, the state needs 2ⁿ × 16 bytes. Adding one qubit doubles memory and time per gate.
concepts.visual_explanation: A vector with 2ⁿ rows that grows as n increases; side panel showing "memory needed" with a slider for n, and a marker for the memory of a typical laptop.
concepts.technical_explanation: Single-precision (8 bytes per amplitude) halves the memory but reduces accuracy; some simulators trade precision for size.
concepts.example: See E01 (memory table) and E02 (a two-qubit Bell circuit done by hand).
concepts.common_mistake: Assuming a simulator can handle "as many qubits as you like". General circuits with more than roughly 30–40 qubits exceed ordinary memory, and about 50 qubits need petabyte-scale memory.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Directly applies Topic 1.2 C06 (exponential state space).
concepts.try_it: Increase n in the memory slider and note where your own machine's memory would run out (Activity A04).
concepts.key_takeaway: A state-vector simulator is exact but needs 2ⁿ amplitudes, so its cost doubles with every added qubit.

concepts.title: Exact Probabilities vs Sampled Shots
concepts.simple_explanation: A simulator can report the *exact* probability of every outcome from the state vector. Both simulators and real hardware can also produce *shots*: individual random outcomes that, collected together, give counts that only approximate the probabilities.
concepts.why_it_matters: Learners often compare "exact" results with "counts" and are confused by differences. Counts fluctuate randomly; the fluctuations shrink slowly as the number of shots grows.
concepts.how_it_works: If an outcome has probability p, then in N shots its measured frequency has standard error √(p(1−p)/N). With more shots the estimate improves, but only as 1/√N — 100 times more shots gives only 10 times smaller error. Real hardware gives only counts; an ideal state-vector simulator can give both.
concepts.visual_explanation: Side-by-side bars: exact probabilities (e.g. 50%/50%) and a histogram of counts that wobbles around them; a slider for number of shots shows the histogram converging.
concepts.technical_explanation: Shot outcomes are independent random samples from the Born-rule distribution P(x) = |c_x|².
concepts.example: See E03: for N = 1,000 shots of a 50/50 outcome, expect about 500 ± 16 (one standard error), and roughly 468–532 for about 95% of runs.
concepts.common_mistake: Expecting exactly 500/500 from 1000 shots, or treating a 490/510 split as evidence that the circuit is wrong.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Extends Topic 1.2 C03 (measurement is probabilistic; repeat to see probabilities).
concepts.try_it: Run the same circuit with 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 shots (Activity A02).
concepts.key_takeaway: A simulator can show exact probabilities; hardware and sampled simulation give counts that fluctuate around them, shrinking only as 1/√N.

concepts.title: What a Simulator Can Show That Hardware Cannot
concepts.simple_explanation: Because a state-vector simulator holds the full state in memory, it can display things no physical device can reveal: the complete set of amplitudes (including phases), the state after each gate, and exact probabilities without sampling.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is a powerful teaching and debugging feature, and it is also why simulator output must not be confused with something a real machine could give you. It explains why a result is "visible" in a lab but "unreadable" on hardware (Topic 1.2, M07).
concepts.how_it_works: A simulator can "save the state vector" at any step. On hardware, measurement is the only way to extract information, and it destroys the superposition; reading out all amplitudes would require preparing the same state very many times and using specialised techniques (state tomography), whose cost grows exponentially with qubit number.
concepts.visual_explanation: A circuit with a "peek inside" marker after each gate in simulator mode, showing amplitude bars (with sign/phase arrows); on the hardware side the same marker is greyed out with the label "not available".
concepts.technical_explanation: Looking inside is a simulator-only feature, so it breaks the rules that apply on real devices.
concepts.mathematical_representation: Simulator output after gate k: |ψ_k⟩ = U_k ⋯ U_1 |ψ_0⟩ (all amplitudes visible).
concepts.example: After H on |0⟩ the simulator can show amplitudes (0.707, 0.707); hardware can only return many 0s and 1s that approximate 50/50.
concepts.common_mistake: Designing an algorithm that "reads the amplitudes" at the end — fine in a simulator, impossible on hardware.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Reinforces Topic 1.2 M07: n qubits have 2ⁿ amplitudes but measurement returns only n bits.
concepts.try_it: Step through the Bell circuit and see the amplitudes after each gate (Activity A01).
concepts.key_takeaway: A simulator lets you look inside the computation; a quantum computer only gives you measurement outcomes.

concepts.title: Why Hardware Results Differ from Ideal Simulation
concepts.simple_explanation: Physical devices introduce imperfections that a noise-free simulator does not model, so results differ from the ideal predictions.
concepts.why_it_matters: When a hardware result looks "wrong", it is usually not a bug in the learner's circuit but a sign of noise or hardware constraints. Learners need to know the main causes.
concepts.how_it_works:
Common sources of difference:
• **Gate errors:** operations are slightly imperfect.
• **Readout errors:** a qubit measured as 0 may be reported as 1 or vice versa.
• **Decoherence:** qubits lose their quantum state over time; longer circuits suffer more.
• **Crosstalk:** operations on one qubit disturb neighbours.
• **Limited connectivity and native gate set:** not every pair of qubits can interact directly, so the circuit is compiled with extra operations (such as swaps), making it longer and noisier.
• **Finite shots:** statistical fluctuation, present even with perfect hardware.
Simulators can include a **noise model** — a mathematical approximation of such errors — to give a more realistic prediction, but it is only a model.
concepts.visual_explanation: An ideal Bell-state histogram (only 00 and 11) beside a noisy one with small bars at 01 and 10, with callouts naming the likely causes.
concepts.technical_explanation: Noise is described by error channels (for example depolarising or readout-flip channels); simulating these requires either repeated random sampling of errors or a density-matrix representation (C07).
concepts.mathematical_representation: Readout error example (illustrative): if a qubit in |0⟩ is misread as 1 with probability e, measured P(1) = e. For e = 0.02, 2% of shots read 1 even for a perfect |0⟩.
concepts.example: A Bell-state circuit on hardware: ideal result 00 ≈ 50%, 11 ≈ 50%, 01 = 10 = 0%. On hardware, 01 and 10 appear with small non-zero probability.
concepts.common_mistake: Concluding that the circuit is wrong, or that entanglement "did not work", because a small number of 01/10 outcomes appear.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Applies Topic 1.3 C08 (NISQ devices; noise and error correction).
concepts.try_it: Raise the noise level in the noisy simulator and watch 01/10 counts appear (Activity A03).
concepts.key_takeaway: Hardware results differ from ideal ones because of noise, decoherence, readout errors, limited connectivity and finite shots; a noise model only approximates this.

concepts.title: Types of Simulators and Circuits That Are Easy to Simulate
concepts.simple_explanation: Different simulation methods trade generality against cost, and some important circuit families can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains why "has entanglement" does not mean "hard to simulate", why simulators can handle certain large circuits, and how classical simulation methods are used to test quantum-advantage claims (Topic 1.3 C08).
concepts.how_it_works:
• **State-vector simulator:** stores 2ⁿ amplitudes; exact; cost doubles per qubit.
• **Density-matrix simulator:** stores a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ matrix, which can represent noisy (mixed) states; memory grows like 4ⁿ, so it reaches fewer qubits.
• **Stabilizer (Clifford) simulator:** simulates circuits made only of Clifford gates (such as H, S and CNOT) with computational-basis input and measurement in time polynomial in n. This is the Gottesman–Knill theorem. These circuits can generate highly entangled states (including Bell and GHZ states) yet remain classically easy. Adding a non-Clifford gate (such as T) breaks this efficiency.
• **Tensor-network / matrix-product-state simulator:** exploits limited entanglement or special structure; efficient when entanglement stays low, expensive when it grows.
Hence classical simulation is hard in general, but easy for special cases. Quantum advantage claims must therefore be compared with the best classical methods, including these ones.
concepts.visual_explanation: A map of four simulator types, each with a "what limits it" label (memory 2ⁿ / memory 4ⁿ / non-Clifford gates / entanglement).
concepts.technical_explanation: Efficiency depends on the structure of the circuit, not only on its qubit count.
concepts.mathematical_representation: State-vector memory ∝ 2ⁿ;  density-matrix memory ∝ 4ⁿ;  stabilizer simulation time ∝ polynomial in n (Clifford circuits).
concepts.example: A 40-qubit GHZ-state circuit (H on q0, then a chain of CNOTs) can be simulated easily by a stabilizer simulator even though a 40-qubit state vector needs 16 TiB (E04).
concepts.common_mistake: Assuming entanglement alone makes a circuit hard to simulate classically.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Builds on Topic 1.2 C07 (entanglement) and Topic 1.3 C08 (advantage claims versus classical baselines).
concepts.try_it: Simulate GHZ states with increasing n using the stabilizer method (Activity A04).
concepts.key_takeaway: General quantum circuits are hard to simulate classically, but structured ones — Clifford circuits or low-entanglement circuits — can be simulated efficiently.

concepts.title: Choosing Between a Simulator and a Quantum Computer
concepts.simple_explanation: A practical decision guide for which tool fits which job.
concepts.why_it_matters: Using hardware for tasks a simulator handles wastes time and adds noise; using a simulator for tasks beyond its reach gives wrong expectations.
concepts.how_it_works: Use a simulator to: learn concepts; design and debug circuits; check ideal outputs; study the effect of a noise model; and test small algorithms. Use real hardware to: observe real noise and errors; benchmark devices; validate that a circuit works under real constraints; and run circuits beyond simulation reach (when large and reliable enough). Typical workflow: design → test on an ideal simulator → test on a noisy simulator → run on hardware → compare with the ideal prediction. Hardware access is typically via the cloud, with queues and limited availability.
concepts.visual_explanation: A workflow diagram of the five steps with a "fastest/cheapest" to "most realistic" gradient bar.
concepts.technical_explanation: Agreement between simulator and hardware outputs, up to expected noise, is evidence that the circuit was implemented correctly.
concepts.example: A learner checks that a 3-qubit circuit produces the expected truth table on a simulator, then runs it on hardware to see how noise changes the counts.
concepts.common_mistake: Believing that "it works on the simulator" guarantees the same output on a real device.
concepts.try_it: Use the decision cards in Example E04 and Activity A01.
concepts.key_takeaway: Develop and debug on simulators; use hardware to learn about real behaviour and to go beyond what simulators can handle.
